title: What I Would Not Pass On

imagePrompt: Create one 1536 x 1024 pixel painted scene sheet, EXACTLY TWO COLUMNS BY THREE ROWS, six equal-width WIDE cinematic panels in row-major order 0 to 5. Each column is 768 pixels; rows are approximately 341, 341 and 342 pixels high. Hard straight cell edges; no gutters, no panel labels, no numbers, no captions, no typography, no readable lettering, no logos. Every cell is its own complete environment, never a sprite or a cutout. Use the polished watercolor and fine ink on textured cream paper style of Enough: warm directional light, deep teal and umber shadows, restrained paper grain, expressive natural faces, subtle imperfect painted edges. Human anatomy is believable, heads naturally sized; shoulders, elbows, wrists, hands, hips and knees belong to one continuous body. Seat hips on the actual seat, feet on the same floor, fingers visibly holding their actual objects; no disembodied hands, duplicated limbs, floating props or pasted-on heads. Keep important faces, hands, contact points and grounded figures within each wide panel with safe margins. Maintain the same identities, clothing, figure scale, prop design and spatial continuity across all six scenes. Anonymous original visual casting only, not likenesses of credited storytellers. This is a dramatic storyboard adaptation, not a claim that imagined symbols or staged details are verified events. Story: What I Would Not Pass On. Palette accents: #F3D6CA, #6A6A87, #EAB475. Identity continuity: GRANDMOTHER: The same older woman with warm tan skin, greying long dark hair, muted purple blouse and slate skirt. Later she is visibly older and receives help, without changing identity or becoming a caricature. MOTHER: The same adult mother with deeper warm brown skin, long dark brown hair, muted rose blouse and slate skirt; firm and caring at once, with distinct face and adult proportions. DAUGHTER: The same young girl with lighter warm brown skin, long brown hair, mustard-yellow top and slate skirt, clearly child-sized. She is protected from criticism, not used as a symbol in place of a person. TOP LEFT (frame 0): Three generations stand near a tall dressing mirror and small wooden table in an ordinary warm room. Place the grandmother left, mother center and daughter right at natural age-relative sizes. The older woman's mouth has begun a criticism, one hand lifted toward the mirror; a single sharp dark empty speech-shape points toward the child. The mother notices its direction. Show only a restrained believable partial mirror reflection, not extra doubled people or distorted bodies. TOP RIGHT (frame 1): The mother steps between grandmother and child with feet firmly planted and one open hand held across the path of the pointed empty speech-shape, fingers relaxed and elbow naturally bent. Her other arm stays near her own body, not grabbing the girl. Her face is steady and direct toward the grandmother, without a retaliatory sneer. The daughter remains clearly behind the boundary, watching. Keep the mirror, table and three distinct connected bodies consistent. MIDDLE LEFT (frame 2): The daughter peeks around the safe edge of the mirror toward her mother, one small hand touching the frame and the other held near her own waist. Her lifted brows and uncertain mouth ask whether she is at fault. The mother turns immediately toward her with full attention, her boundary hand now lowered. The grandmother stays in the background at ordinary scale. Do not frame the child as guilty or leave her frightened beneath a giant adult hand. MIDDLE RIGHT (frame 3): The mother crouches naturally to the daughter's eye level, one knee bent and balanced on a real foot, both hands open low near her own knees. She gives the child a clear warm face; the daughter begins to release her grip on the mirror and look back. The grandmother is present at a respectful distance, not banished or monstrous. The pointed speech-shape has stopped beside the mother and cannot reach the girl. No idealized beauty image appears in the mirror. BOTTOM LEFT (frame 4): The mother stands beside the table and sets a small folded dark paper-like speech-shape flat on its surface, wrist and fingertips touching it in one coherent gentle action. The pointed edge no longer aims at anyone. The daughter stands freely beside the mirror with hands relaxed and a small secure expression. The grandmother watches in thoughtful silence from the other side. Their ordinary clothes and the room remain unchanged; the visual metaphor is contained, not weaponized. BOTTOM RIGHT (frame 5): A restrained later scene in a quieter corner of a domestic room: the same grandmother, visibly older but recognizable, sits firmly in a supportive chair. The mother stands beside her offering one hand for balance, their actual palms meeting naturally. Her other hand is a small open boundary gesture near her own waist, her face gentle and firm. Keep the folded dark shape set aside on a distant table. No child substitute, no diagnosis, no implied forgiveness that erases the boundary. Story-specific safeguards: The later grandmother is the same person, not the daughter aged into a replacement role. The later care does not annul the mother's boundary. No appearance correction, beauty ideal, abusive spectacle, diagnosis or retaliatory cruelty is added.
